Senses.Explanation: Literally, "one blade-stroke, two pieces" (一刀兩段); in its primary Chan deployment, "a decisive cut." The phrase occurs 224 times in 106 allowlisted texts. It is used as a compact answer, imperative, appraisal, and description of a person. Asked whether something is "spiritual power and wondrous function, naturally just so" (神通妙用，法爾如然), a master answers only, "a decisive cut" (一刀兩段). Dahui tells a reader to do it directly in ordinary daily activity, followed by "start from beneath your heels; there is no need to set the mind waiting for awakening" (便從脚跟下做將去，不必將心等悟). Another discourse says that one who wants to clarify this matter must be "a person of one cut, two pieces" (一刀兩段漢). The record also checks the formula: "one cut, two pieces—still not worthy of a lineage teacher" (一刀兩段，未稱宗師). The corpus thus gives the cutting formula a place in Chan answers and appraisals but does not authorize an added claim about what mental or spiritual object is cut.
Senses.Note: This sense is separated from an attested literal execution request below. Different figurative readings of the same cutting formula are not multiplied into senses.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The phrase is the master's entire answer to a follow-up about spiritual power and wondrous function.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui gives the formula as a direct imperative and immediately says to proceed from beneath one's heels without setting the mind to await awakening.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to cut in two with one stroke
Senses.Explanation: The same four graphs can name an actual bodily cutting into two pieces with one stroke. In a bandit episode, the monk says, "now is just the right time; please cut me in two with one stroke," and then cries, "cut! cut!" (如今正好乘時，便請一刀兩段，乃大呼斬斬). This concrete execution request is a different event from using the phrase as an answer or appraisal, so it receives its own corpus-wide sense.
Senses.Note: One defining allowlisted narrative is curated for this literal sense. Other apparent concrete uses must be checked passage by passage rather than inferred from the phrase alone.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如今正好乘時，便請一刀兩段。乃大呼：斬！斬！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Facing bandits, the monk requests literal cutting into two and shouts, "cut! cut!"

Senses.Explanation: Literally, everything (一切) is already complete or ready-made (現成). The phrase enters the Chan record in Dizang's answer to Fayan: when discussing the buddha teaching, everything is already complete. Later records quote that exchange and list “everything is already complete” as the characteristic wording of the Fayan house. It also appears as an answer to “What is the Fayan house?” and in Dahui's instruction to step back, look for oneself, and directly take responsibility for what is already complete. The record does not treat the formula as a licence for mere repetition: Lushan Tianran asks whether saying it would mean an entire summer had passed in vain, while another exchange answers a student's repetition with blows and “Do not cite this wrongly to people.” The Chan deviation is therefore a house formula, answer, and contested quotation attached to the Dizang–Fayan encounter, not merely the ordinary statement that supplies are ready.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 73 exact occurrences in 48 allowlisted files. The phrase is repeatedly quoted as Dizang's answer to Fayan, classified as Fayan-house wording, used as an answer, and challenged when merely asserted.

Senses.PreferredTarget: drink up all the West River's water in one mouthful
AlternateTargets: draw all the West River's water into one mouthful
drink the West River dry in one mouthful
Senses.Explanation: A line from Layman Pang's recorded exchange with Mazu. Pang asks, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' Mazu answers, 'When you drink up all the West River's water in one mouthful, I will tell you.' Later records quote the speaker turns, make the line a question in its own right, answer it, and write verses or comments on it. Yuanwu, when asked what about drinking up the river, answers, 'The bright sun adorns the sky.' Another teacher sets the West River line aside and asks the master to swallow the mounting platform in front of the steps; the master spreads both hands and says, 'Bring it here carefully.' A verse says that after the river is drunk in one mouthful, no drop remains through all antiquity, then remarks that Mazu's mouth was unfortunately narrow. These are the record's observable continuations of the original exchange.
Senses.Note: The exact line has 329 matches in 139 files; the shorter opening 'in one mouthful drink up all' has 398 matches in 153. Mazu's full conditional 'when you drink up all the West River's water in one mouthful' occurs 151 times in 95 files. No required definition formula occurs. The preserved witnesses include the founding exchange, verse commentary, a new test modeled on the line, Yuanwu's direct answer, a later address extending the river image to the bottom of a deep pool, and another master's replacement answer. The phrase remains a line spoken in a named public case and a subject of later public questioning.

Senses.Explanation: One phrase, clause, line, or saying counted as a unit of speech. Chan records weight this ordinary unit through where it stands and what is done with it, without making every phrase mean the same thing. Linji is asked for “the first phrase” and separately says that a single phrase must contain three mysterious gates, each with three essentials, authority, and function. Later records repeat that a single phrase plainly encompasses the myriad forms. Blue Cliff commentary says that penetrating one phrase penetrates a thousand and ten thousand phrases at once and quotes a line in which one phrase clearly understood surpasses a hundred billion. A verse contrasts three thousand recited scripture sections with “one phrase of Caoxi,” while Layman Pang says that even one phrase is unnecessary in an exchange. Other recurrent positions and qualifications include a silent phrase posed as a question, an “out-of-pattern phrase” demanded after a pause, and a ceremonial house phrase that the speaker asks how to voice. The diminutive “one phrase” (一句子) can be something a master says he has never told anyone. The cited warning “one conforming phrase is a donkey-tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas” appraises a kind of phrase without defining every instance of the headword that way. The Zen bend is therefore the phrase's deployment as the smallest publicly tested or house-qualified unit that can be raised, withheld, penetrated, ranked, capped, or challenged. First, second, third, final, upward, out-of-pattern, and conforming positions belong to the same countable speech unit unless a longer fixed term has its own entry.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 15,708 occurrences in 419 texts. Family checks covered “first phrase” (第一句), “second phrase” (第二句), “third phrase” (第三句), “final phrase” (末後一句) and its shorter form (末後句), “upward phrase” (向上一句), “out-of-pattern phrase” (出格一句), the diminutive “one phrase” (一句子), “one conforming phrase” (一句合頭語), “under one phrase” (一句下), “a thousand and ten thousand phrases” (千句萬句), and the general “phrase” entry (句). Item-8 review found position and qualification families, not different objects: verse line, spoken phrase, quoted saying, and section-qualified phrase remain countable utterance units in the harvested passages. Twelve exact-headword witnesses replace the former thin set; two former KWICs that contained only the shorter “final phrase” form (末後句), rather than the exact headword “one phrase” (一句), were removed. No occurrence is retained merely to support an interpretive meaning for an unspecified phrase.

Senses.Explanation: A single (一) shout (喝): “a single shout.” The headword occurs 12,565 times across 377 allowlisted texts, while the verbal form “give a shout” occurs 7,091 times across 320 texts. In the public interview a shout answers or challenges a question, meets hesitation, is exchanged and evaluated by master and monk, or closes a hall address before the speaker steps down. Linji's record states four comparisons: a shout may be like the jeweled sword of a Vajra king, like a gold-maned lion crouching on the ground, like a probing pole and shadowing grass, or not used as a shout. Xinghua Cunjiang's record contains a case in which the elder Minde is said to understand “a shout not used as a shout.” Another recurrent verse says, “A single shout divides guest and host; illumination and function proceed at once”; the records attribute this verse to the old man of Guyin, not to Linji. The fixed pairing “Deshan's staff, Linji's shout” places the vocal act beside the staff. In the Mazu–Baizhang case, Baizhang recalls that one shout from Master Ma left him deaf for three days. These records classify and deploy the same audible act; they do not turn every shout into one hidden meaning.
Senses.Note: Keep the textual attributions separate. Linji is the source represented here for the four comparisons. The Minde case occurs in Xinghua Cunjiang's section. The verse about dividing guest and host is raised under Guyin's name, not Linji's. The staff-and-shout pairing circulates as a stock saying. Compare “shout” and “staff and shout.”

Senses.Explanation: Literally, one dust-speck. The expression occurs 1,830 times in 293 allowlisted texts. It serves as the smallest named particle in descriptions of scale and inclusion, especially the formulas 'one speck contains the whole field' and 'within one speck.' It also enters negative formulas: 'not establish one speck,' 'not stained by one speck,' and 'before one speck is raised.' In direct exchanges, answers to 'What is one speck?' include 'the nine ages divided into an instant,' 'it is you,' and 'without noticing, it becomes a hill or mountain.' One lamp record explicitly says that, in its cited saying about a great scroll inside a minute particle, one speck is one thought-speck.
Senses.Note: The evidence retains the graph's concrete small-scale image and records the corpus's extensions without replacing it with an abstract system. Audit counts include 94 instances of 'not establish one speck,' 20 of 'not stained by one speck,' 114 of 'within one speck,' and 59 exact 'What is one speck?' questions.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the one great matter (for which the Buddhas appear in the world)
Senses.Explanation: (一大事) = the one great matter; (因緣) = occasion / cause-and-condition. The phrase originates in the Lotus Sūtra — (諸佛世尊唯以一大事因緣故出現於世), 'the Buddhas appear in the world solely for the one great matter' — and the Chan corpus keeps that source-wording: (一大事因緣) stands within eight characters of (出現於世) in 97 places across 68 allowlist files, and the frame (為一大事因緣) occurs 199 times in 100 files. The corpus glosses the term in its own words: the Platform Sutra has (經云)：『(諸佛世尊)，(唯以一大事因緣出現於世)。』(一大事者)，(佛之知見也) ('the one great matter is the Buddha's knowing-and-seeing'), and (禪源諸詮集都序) has (一大事者)。(欲令眾生開佛知見)。(乃至入佛知見道故) ('the one great matter: to have beings open the Buddha's knowing-and-seeing, up to entering the way of the Buddha's knowing-and-seeing'). Three attested deployments. (1) Said of the patriarchs and of the living master as of the Buddhas: (佛出世)。(提持一大事因緣)。(祖師西來) (Yuanwu), and (博山出世亦為一大事因緣) — Wuyi Yuanlai says it of his own appearance in the world. (2) Posed as a question — (如何是一大事因緣) ('what is the one great matter?') occurs 59 times in 27 files; in (景德傳燈錄) Touzi answers it (尹司空為老僧開堂) ('Vice-Director Yin opened the hall for me'). (3) Said of the correspondent's own work — Dahui writes to a layman (知為此一大事因緣甚力) ('I know you are working at this one great matter with great force').
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense: the same phrase is attested of the Buddhas' appearing, of patriarchs and living masters, as the question (如何是一大事因緣), and of the recipient's own work in letters — kept as a single sense. Pan-Buddhist in origin (Lotus) but the curated evidence is Chan usage only. Well attested: 415 raw hits across 152 allowlist files (tag-stripped grep, 2026-07-11). Attribution guarded: two front-matter occurrences in (大慧語錄) were REJECTED — 0813a23 sits under (進大慧禪師語錄奏劄) (a memorial-to-throne preface by the submitting official) and 0842c13 under (大慧普覺禪師塔銘) (his post-mortem stupa epitaph); neither is Dahui's own words. The cited Dahui occurrence (0936c03) is inside his own letter (答黃知縣子餘).

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是一大事因緣。師曰。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄); two-speaker Q&A (問 / 師曰), MasterName=null per the two-speaker rule. The entry stands under (前京兆翠微無學禪師法嗣), i.e. Touzi Datong (投子大同, heir of Cuiwei Wuxue, in master-dates.json); his reply on the next line is (尹司空為老僧開堂) ('Vice-Director Yin opened the hall for me'). Kwic trimmed to the single source line (answer crosses the <lb>).

Occurrences.Kwic: 知為此一大事因緣甚力。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (大慧普覺禪師語錄), head (答黃知縣子餘) — Dahui's own reply-letter, using the phrase of the layman's own work (為此一大事因緣甚力).

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘one-word barrier.’ The phrase occurs 71 times in 49 allowlisted texts. The Human and Celestial Eyes supplies the corpus's naming formula: after examples of Yunmen answering prompts with a single graph—‘ancestor’ to ‘what is Yunmen's sword?,’ ‘mound’ to ‘what is within the mysterious?,’ ‘bones’ or ‘a corpse’ to ‘what is the hair-blown sword?,’ and ‘everywhere’ to ‘what is the eye of the true teaching?’—it says that Yunmen often responded to encounters this way, ‘therefore the monasteries named it the one-word barrier.’ Later texts consequently pair ‘Yunmen's one-word barrier’ with Linji's three mysteries, Caoshan's three falls, and other house-associated rosters. A later verse repeats ‘one-word barrier’ and asks why it remains single rather than becoming a pair. The term names the rostered one-word response, not every ordinary barrier containing one written character.
Senses.Note: Zen bends ordinary ‘one word’ plus ‘barrier’ language into the monastic name for Yunmen's recurrent single-graph answers. The naming formula is explicit, so this deviation is corpus-stated. Cross-check with ‘look—look!—hah!’ (顧鑒咦): one later text says the shortened ‘look!—hah!’ became a one-word barrier, but that later comparison does not make the two labels identical or create a second sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 故叢林目之。曰一字關云。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After listing Yunmen's single-graph answers, the text explicitly says: ‘therefore the monasteries named it the one-word barrier.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 一字關一字關僧問師。如何是雲門劍。師云祖
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The roster begins ‘one-word barrier’ and records: a monk asks ‘what is Yunmen's sword?’; Yunmen says ‘ancestor.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 有人透得此關，許他親見雲門。」頌：「一字關、一字關，何不成雙獨成單？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later comment says that one who passes this barrier may personally see Yunmen; its verse repeats ‘one-word barrier’ and asks why it is single rather than paired.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “not one thought arises.” The phrase is quoted in Zhang Zhuo's verse, “not a single thought arises—the whole body appears; the six faculties barely move and clouds cover it.” Yuanwu places it beside resting, not falling into sense-objects, and not dwelling in conceptual imagining. Yongjue gives an explicit explanation: “this mind functions yet is constantly still, is still yet constantly functions,” and says one's thoughts remain apart from encountered objects. The records also subject the phrase to public testing. A monk asks Yunmen whether not a single thought arising still has a fault; Yunmen answers “Mount Sumeru.” Xuedou later asks Zhimen why it has a fault and is struck when he comes forward. The headword occurs 385 times across 152 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide phrase; its affirmative use and its interrogation are different deployments of the same state, not different things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一念不生全體現，六根纔動被雲遮
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yongjue quotes Zhang Zhuo's verse: the whole body appears when not one thought arises, while movement of the six faculties brings clouding.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一念不生者，此心用而常寂，寂而常用，祇於自念上常離諸境
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yongjue explicitly defines the phrase as mind functioning while still and remaining apart from encountered objects in its own thoughts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 唯是休歇到一念不生處，則便透脫，不墮情塵，不居意想
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's letter uses the phrase in an instruction, alongside resting and not dwelling in conceptual imagining.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問雲門一念不生還有過也無門云須彌山
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public case asks Yunmen whether not one thought arising still has a fault; he answers Mount Sumeru.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪竇顯禪師問智門云一念不生為甚麼有過門召近前竇近前門便打
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later exchange records Xuedou asking Zhimen why the state has a fault and being struck when he approaches.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, "one-finger Chan." The phrase names Juzhi's recorded use of a raised finger in public interviews. A later record states the visible rule directly: "Whenever someone came, Master Juzhi only extended one finger; he called it one-finger Chan" (俱胝和尚逢人但伸一指頭，喚做一指頭禪). In the transmitted case, Tianlong raises one finger to Juzhi; afterward, whenever students ask, Juzhi raises one finger, and before dying he says, "I obtained Tianlong's one-finger Chan; through my whole life I could not use it up" (吾得天龍一指頭禪，一生用不盡). The record also preserves criticism rather than making the label an unquestioned formula: Xuansha says he would have broken the finger, Caoshan faults Juzhi's taking it up, and Sanshan asks, "What connection does one-finger Chan have? It cheated that monk and buried him alive his whole life" (一指頭禪有甚交涉？賺殺阿僧終身活埋). Its Chan-specific bend is thus a named, publicly repeated response inherited from Tianlong and continually examined by later masters.
Senses.Note: Attested 80 times in 50 allowlisted texts. "Juzhi's one finger" (俱胝一指) names the case/action family; "one-finger Chan" (一指頭禪) is the label Juzhi claims for what he received from Tianlong. The same referent is praised, questioned, and criticized; differing appraisals are readings of one recorded deployment, not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 俱胝和尚逢人但伸一指頭，喚做一指頭禪。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later record gives the direct naming formula: Juzhi extended one finger to visitors and called it one-finger Chan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 吾得天龍一指頭禪，一生用不盡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juzhi's own closing claim names Tianlong as the source and says a lifetime did not use it up.

Occurrences.Kwic: 後凡有所問。只豎一指。每曰。我得天龍一指頭禪。一生受用不盡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's record joins the public-question deployment to Juzhi's repeated claim.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一指頭禪有甚交涉？賺殺阿僧終身活埋。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Sanshan explicitly challenges the phrase and says it cheated and buried the monk alive.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一指頭禪誰不有？靈樞妙轉在天龍
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse asks who does not have one-finger Chan and locates its deft turning in Tianlong.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a day without work is a day without food
AlternateTargets: if I do not work for a day, I do not eat for a day
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “one day not working, one day not eating.” The Chan institutional record attributes the saying to Baizhang and ties it to shared manual labor: the monastic regulations say that even in old age he “shared the community's labor” (與眾均其勞) and regularly said the line. The same regulations later call it “the warning of the ancients” (古人之誡) when directing the community to attend communal work. Xutang's record adds that at age ninety-five Baizhang's hoe, cutting tool, rain cape, and bamboo hat never left him. Hongzhi quotes the saying and calls “farming to obtain food to eat” (種田博飯喫) “the house style” (家風). Its Zen deviation is institutional and explicit: a maxim attached to Baizhang becomes the recorded house rule for the teacher's and community's agricultural labor.
Senses.Note: The exact saying occurs 8 times in 6 allowlisted texts. Independent witnesses preserve attribution to Baizhang, its later status as an injunction for communal labor, and Hongzhi's house-style quotation. No competing wording establishes a separate sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 至於作務。猶與眾均其勞。常曰。一日不作一日不食。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Baizhang monastic regulations say that he shared the community's labor and regularly said, “A day without work is a day without food.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 並宜齊赴。當思古人一日不作一日不食之誡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The communal-work section tells all eligible residents to attend and remember the ancient's warning, “a day without work is a day without food.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日不作一日不食。歇者無心穫者力。分明只箇是家風。會得種田博飯喫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi quotes the maxim, calls it “the house style,” and follows it with “farming to obtain food to eat.”

AlternateTargets: where does the one go back to?
to where does the one return?
Senses.Explanation: A four-graph question: 'the one' (一) + 'returns' (歸) + 'what place?' (何處): 'where does the one return?' The allowlisted record has 755 occurrences in 203 texts. It normally follows 'the ten thousand things return to one' (萬法歸一), producing the complete question, 'the ten thousand things return to one; where does the one return?' (萬法歸一，一歸何處). The best-known public case records a monk asking Zhaozhou this question and Zhaozhou replying, 'when I was in Qingzhou, I made a cloth shirt weighing seven catties' (我在青州作一領布衫，重七斤). The question is not confined to that exchange: a Hongzhi address places beside it a second record in which Wenshu answers, 'the Yellow River's nine bends' (黃河九曲); the Lamp Record gives Baizhang Mingzhao's answer, 'there has not been one who did not ask' (未有一箇不問). Later masters use the question as an entire address, put it to monks in the room, quote Zhaozhou's answer when testing a response, and record their own answers, including 'in the land of Silla' (新羅國裏) and 'today is as hot as yesterday' (今日熱如昨日). The entry preserves the literal question and its documented answer-history without choosing among the recorded replies.
Senses.Note: Corpus counts: 'where does the one return?' (一歸何處), 755 hits in 203 texts; 'the ten thousand things return to one' (萬法歸一), 852/219; the punctuated complete question (萬法歸一，一歸何處), 438/150; the unpunctuated complete question (萬法歸一一歸何處), 41/16; 'what is where-the-one-returns?' (如何是一歸何處), 7/6; and nominal 'one asking where the one returns' (一歸何處者), 2/2. No equation-style self-definition was found. The phrase is a stock question with multiple recorded respondents and later comments, not a master-specific sense; SenseKey therefore remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉。僧問趙州。萬法歸一。一歸何處。州云。我在青州作一領布衫。重七斤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu Keqin raises the Zhaozhou case in his comments on old cases: 'a monk asked Zhaozhou, "the ten thousand things return to one; where does the one return?" Zhaozhou said, "when I was in Qingzhou, I made a cloth shirt weighing seven catties."' It is a raised case, so MasterName is null; the named respondent is Zhaozhou Congshen.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂舉僧問趙州。萬法歸一。一歸何處。州云。我在青州。作一領布衫重七斤。又僧問文殊。萬法歸一。一歸何處。殊云。黃河九曲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi Zhengjue raises two records side by side: Zhaozhou's seven-catty cloth shirt and Wenshu's 'the Yellow River's nine bends.' Because both are quoted cases within Hongzhi's address, MasterName is null rather than cross-attributing the KWIC to one speaker.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問萬法歸一一歸何處。師曰。未有一箇不問。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Lamp Record (景德傳燈錄), under Baizhang Mingzhao An, the question is asked without punctuation between its two clauses. He replies, 'there has not been one who did not ask.' The roster has no exact linkable spelling for Baizhang Mingzhao An.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：萬法歸一，一歸何處？乃顧視左右，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Gaofeng Yuanmiao's own record. His complete address is: 'the ten thousand things return to one; where does the one return?' He then looks left and right and leaves the seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 室中問僧：萬法歸一，一歸何處？曰：新羅國裏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), under Lan'an Dingxu, the master puts the question to a monk in the room; the monk answers, 'in the land of Silla.' The named master lacks an exact roster spelling.

Occurrences.Kwic: 忽有僧問：萬法歸一，一歸何處？只向他道：今日熱如昨日。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Draft Continuation of the Lamp (續燈存稿), Zhuquan Liaohuan Falin says that if a monk asked the stock question, he would answer, 'today is as hot as yesterday.' The named master lacks an exact roster spelling.

Senses.Explanation: The numeral "one" (一) plus "thing" or "object" (物): "one thing," attested 2,625 times in 353 allowlisted texts. Its Chan deployment includes positive, negative, indefinite, and deliberately unnamed forms. In the Nanyue-Huineng encounter, Nanyue says that "to describe it as one thing would not hit it" (說似一物即不中), after eight years of inquiry. Huineng's verse says, "awakening originally has no tree; the bright mirror is not a stand; originally there is not one thing; where could dust alight?" (菩提本無樹，明鏡亦非臺，本來無一物，何處惹塵埃). A lamp question quotes, "the hundred bones all collapse and scatter; one thing remains constantly numinous—what is the one thing?" and receives "what suffering, buddha!" (百骸俱潰散，一物鎮長靈；如何是一物；苦哉佛陀耶). Another address says, "outside, not one thing can establish [anything]; all are the original mind producing ten thousand kinds of things" (外無一物而能建立，皆是本心生萬種法). Later speakers also challenge anyone "not relying on one thing" (不依倚一物). These records use the ordinary noun precisely: sometimes an unnamed referent is proposed, sometimes even that label is rejected, and sometimes the phrase negates every external thing.
Senses.Note: Counted constructions: "originally not one thing" (本來無一物), 214; "to describe it as one thing would not hit it" (說似一物即不中), 105; "there is one thing" (有一物), 385; "not one thing" (無一物), 918; "not rely on one thing" (不依倚一物), 69. These contrasting constructions do not justify turning "one thing" into a fixed metaphysical entity.

Occurrences.Kwic: 說似一物即不中祖云還假修證也無
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Nanyue-Huineng exchange: Nanyue says, "to describe it as one thing would not hit it." Huineng then asks whether cultivation and verification are still required. Two-speaker case, so unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 菩提本無樹。明鏡亦非臺。本來無一物。何處惹塵埃。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huineng's verse in the Compendium of Five Lamps: "awakening originally has no tree; the bright mirror is not a stand; originally there is not one thing; where could dust alight?"

Occurrences.Kwic: 百骸俱潰散一物鎮長靈。如何是一物。師曰。苦哉佛陀耶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks: "the hundred bones all collapse and scatter; one thing remains constantly numinous. What is the one thing?" The master answers, "what suffering, buddha!" The monk's headword-bearing turn remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 外無一物而能建立。皆是本心生萬種法。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Transmission-lamp address: "outside, not one thing can establish [anything]; all are the original mind producing ten thousand kinds of things." Historical section remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 九十日內不依倚一物者不妨請出
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shiguan's address challenges: "within the ninety days, anyone who does not rely on one thing may please come out." No validated roster link is used.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “not hanging a single thread”: not wearing even one strand of clothing. The late Chan records deploy nakedness as a description of a person after successive stripping: Xueguan compares it to taking off clothes and undoing a belt, layer after layer, then asks what could still be removed from “a fellow not wearing a single thread” (一絲不掛的漢子). Other records pair the phrase with “coming and going freely” (來去自如) or with “the myriad forms all manifest” (萬象齊彰). The Zen bend is therefore directly visible in its use as an appraisal of a person rather than only a state of undress. The records do not define an inner state behind the image, and this entry does not supply one.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase occurs 10 times in 9 allowlisted texts. The witnesses are concentrated in seventeenth-century records, so the sense is multi-text but late. Searches found the clothing comparison, person-appraisal, paired predicates, and no morphological variant or independent formula that establishes another sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 忽有箇一絲不掛的漢子出來，還教伊脫箇甚麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xueguan's record asks: “If a fellow not wearing a single thread suddenly came out, what would you still have him take off?” The preceding lines explicitly compare the stripping to removing clothing and a belt layer by layer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一絲不掛來去自如？仰望洪慈，策其末路。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Feiyin's record asks of “not wearing a single thread, coming and going freely.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 一絲不掛，萬象齊彰。性相融通，自它俱利。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A robe-subscription text pairs “not wearing a single thread” with “the myriad forms all manifest.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 不惟善能解脫塵勞一絲不掛，且爾直入無上菩提如箭射鵠、如刀破竹
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A prose instruction in Xueguan's record places the phrase between “freed from dusty toil” and comparisons to an arrow striking its target and a knife splitting bamboo.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, one stalk or blade of grass. The Chan corpus loads this smallest ordinary object through a set of reversible public formulas. Most prominently, a master may 'take a single blade of grass and make it a sixteen-foot golden body, and take the sixteen-foot golden body and make it a single blade of grass.' The same blade can found a monastery or display jeweled halls and jade palaces. Baiyun Duan's saying makes the relation reversible: after one true sweat, jeweled halls appear atop a blade of grass; without it, even jeweled halls are covered by the blade. Dahui accepts the first clause but warns that the second may deceive the hearer. A separate inherited encounter supplies another deployment: Sudhana picks a blade of grass from the ground as the medicine requested by Manjusri, who says that this medicine can kill and can give life. The Chan-specific bend lies in how the records repeatedly place the concrete blade in reversible comparison with a buddha-body, a monastery, palaces, and medicine, while later masters quote, test, and qualify those formulas.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist count: 617 hits in 174 texts. Searches covered the golden-body reversal, monastery erection, palace manifestation/covering, medicine case, later qualification, and ordinary botanical use. Family check with the sixteen-foot golden body (丈六金身), monastery (梵剎), jeweled halls and jade palaces (瓊樓玉殿), medicine (藥), and mustard seed (芥子) supports one concrete blade deployed in distinct comparisons, not separate referents; no split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拈一莖草作丈六金身，將丈六金身作一莖草
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The central reversible formula: make a sixteen-foot golden body from one blade of grass, then make the golden body into one blade.

Occurrences.Kwic: 善財遂於地上拈一莖草，度與文殊。殊接得，示眾曰：此藥亦能殺人，亦能活人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Sudhana picks up one blade and hands it to Manjusri, who calls the medicine able both to kill and give life.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何能拈一莖草作丈六金身，插一莖草而建梵剎，向一莖草上現瓊樓玉殿耶？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Enumeration: golden body, founding a monastery, and displaying jeweled halls and jade palaces upon one blade.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若端的得一回汗出，便向一莖草上現出瓊樓玉殿；若未端的得一回汗出，縱有瓊樓玉殿，被一莖草葢却。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baiyun Duan's reversible palace formula: palaces appear upon the blade, or are covered by it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一莖草上現瓊樓玉殿。決定可信。瓊樓玉殿被一莖草蓋却。莫被他熱謾。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui affirms the palace appearing on grass but warns against being deceived by the reverse clause.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "one" (一) "move, placement, or stroke" (著): "one move," attested 3,121 times in 351 allowlisted texts. The game-like noun appears in recurring Chan compounds: "let one move pass" (放過一著, 617 occurrences), "the final move" (末後一著, 104), "the upward move" (向上一著, 279), "one move ahead" (先一著, 38), and the suffixed "one move" (一著子, 601). A case-comment collection appraises an earlier response as "precisely letting one move pass," then adds "danger" (正是放過一著；險). A lamp address pairs "Linji's vanguard—let one move pass" with "Deshan's later command—set it aside" (臨濟先鋒，放過一著；德山後令，且在一邊). Questions ask, "before living beings and buddhas arose, where did one move fall?" (生佛未興時，一著落在甚麼處). Feiyin says, "present one move face to face; the person concerned must personally take it up" (覿面提持個一著，當人要在親領略). These uses support the ordinary move/play sense while showing its Chan deployment as question, appraisal, sequence, and named move.
Senses.Note: The headword retains the concrete move vocabulary rather than being inflated into an unstated realization. The texts themselves qualify moves as final, upward, prior, or passed over. Apparent "one-move is..." formula hits were mostly grammatical "one who singles out the upward move" and are not self-definitions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正是放過一著。復云：險。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Case commentary: "this is precisely letting one move pass." It then adds, "danger." The quoted appraisal remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟先鋒，放過一著。德山後令，且在一邊。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunfeng Wenyue's section: "Linji's vanguard—let one move pass; Deshan's later command—set it aside." Multi-master comparison remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 生佛未興時，一著落在甚麼處？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Huqiu Shaolong's section, a monk asks: "before living beings and buddhas arose, where did one move fall?" It is the monk's turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 覿面提持個一著，當人要在親領略
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Feiyin's address: "present one move face to face; the person concerned must personally take it up." No validated roster link is used.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單提向上一著者。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianru Weize's Lineage Essentials refers to "one who singles out the upward move." This is a productive qualified form, not a self-definition.

AlternateTargets: complete command of the single conduct
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “one act” or “single conduct” (一行) plus “complete command” (三昧). In the Chan corpus Huineng's Platform Record supplies the governing definitions and the Zen-specific correction. It defines the term as “at all times, while walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, constantly carrying a straightforward mind” (於一切時中，行住坐臥，常行直心), and again as carrying a straightforward mind without attachment to anything (於一切法上，無有執著). The Record of the Patriarchal Hall gives the parallel: “in every place, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, all is one straightforward mind; this is the site of the way, this is the pure land” (於一切處行住坐臥，皆一直心，即是道場，即是淨土). The Platform Record then identifies and rejects a contrary deployment: people attached to the term say that sitting without moving and suppressing thoughts is “complete command in one act”; the text says that if so, this is the same as insentient things and an obstructing condition (同無情，却是障道因緣). This explicit correction is the entry's central Zen bend: the named “one act” is defined across all four postures and straightforward mind, not reduced to unmoving sitting. A preface to another Platform edition also defines it as “the single aspect of the realm of things” (法界一相) and says that although the many good acts differ, all are made correct in one act (萬善雖殊，皆正於一行).
Senses.Note: The English translates the final two graphs as “complete command,” as required by the termbase standard; they are not left as an unexplained religious loanword. The direct Huineng definitions and corrective passage are primary. Later lamp witnesses independently preserve the same four-posture and straightforward-mind wording but are historically dependent retellings, so validation rests on multiple allowlisted texts while that dependence is stated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一行三昧者，於一切時中，行、住、坐、臥，常行直心是。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Early Platform Record; Huineng's direct graph-level definition across the four postures.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但行直心，於一切法上，無有執著，名一行三昧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same Platform Record supplies a second direct definition: straightforward mind without attachment to anything.

Occurrences.Kwic: 迷人著法相，執一行三昧，直言坐不動，除妄不起心，即是一行三昧。若如是，此法同無情，却是障道因緣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Platform Record's explicit rejected definition: unmoving sitting and suppressing thoughts are compared to insentient things. This is retained as indispensable corrective evidence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一行三昧者，於一切處行住坐臥，皆一直心，即是道場，即是淨土。此之名為一行三昧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of the Patriarchal Hall retelling of Huineng's definition; a distinct early textual witness linking all four postures, straightforward mind, the site of the way, and pure land.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若於一切處行住坐臥。純一直心不動道場真成淨土。名一行三昧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jingde Lamp Record retelling; preserves the “purely one straightforward mind” form and the same four-posture definition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一行三昧者，法界一相之謂也。謂萬善雖殊，皆正於一行者也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Preface to the Platform Record; a separate direct formula defining the expression through “one aspect of the realm of things” and the many good acts being corrected in one act. It is a preface, not Huineng's attributed speech.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘one arrowhead pierces three checkpoints.’ In Qinshan Wensui's exchange, Juliang asks what it is like when one arrow pierces three checkpoints; Qinshan answers, ‘release the master within the checkpoints and let me see.’ After Juliang calls it a good arrow shot in the wrong place, Qinshan seizes him and says to set piercing three checkpoints aside and shoot an arrow for Qinshan; Juliang hesitates and is struck seven times. Yunmen gives the whole phrase as his own answer after asking how to undertake ‘covering heaven and earth, weighing the coming mechanism to the fraction’ without involving worldly conditions and receiving no answer from the assembly. Later teaching-seat records take up the same archery line with staffs, calling it a flash-like edge, and verse uses it as a closing line. The Zen bend is the military checkpoint-and-arrow formula's repeated use as an answer, challenge, and teaching-seat line in public encounter. The records do not define a universal set of three checkpoints here, so this entry does not substitute Huanglong's or Doushuai's named threes.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense: the literal question, answer-line, and later quotation all name the same arrow/checkpoint event. The distinct Huanglong and Doushuai taxonomies belong under “three barriers” (三關) and are not silently read into this formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一鏃破三關時如何？師曰：放出關中主看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juliang asks the formula as a public question; Qinshan asks to see the master inside the checkpoints.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一鏃破三關即且置，試為欽山發箭看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Qinshan sets the formula aside and demands an arrow shot for himself.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不涉世緣，作麼生承當？眾無對。自代曰：一鏃破三關。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen supplies the phrase as his own answer when the assembly gives none.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一鏃破三關，機鋒如掣電。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later teaching-seat line pairs the formula with an edge like flashing lightning.

Senses.Explanation: Literally "one" (一) classifier (隻) "eye" (眼): "one eye," attested 992 times in 233 allowlisted texts. The records use it in appraisals with the verbs possess, place, lose, exchange, and open. In the Damei case, Jiashan says, "at Damei I lost one eye" (我當時在大梅，失却一隻眼); Xuedou comments that Jiashan did not know he had then "exchanged for one eye" (換得一隻眼). Another appraisal says Yunmen "possesses only one eye" because he "only looks ahead and does not look behind" (只具一隻眼，只管瞻前，不管照後). Productive forms include "possess one eye" (具一隻眼, 381 occurrences), "place one eye here" (著得一隻眼, 89), "lose one eye" (失却一隻眼, 91), and "open another eye" (別開一隻眼).
Senses.Note: The phrase can expand beyond an individual appraisal. Xuefeng says, "the whole earth is a patch-robed monk's one eye" (盡大地是沙門一隻眼). Other instructions say that placing one eye at a cited point lets one "see seven ways vertically and eight ways horizontally" (便見七縱八橫), or that a staff "opens another eye" for the assembly. The corpus records these predicates and images without supplying a single replacement gloss for eye.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我當時在大梅，失却一隻眼。雪竇云：夾山畢竟不知當時換得一隻眼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Raised Damei case and Xuedou's comment: Jiashan says he lost one eye; Xuedou says he did not know he exchanged for one eye.

Occurrences.Kwic: 盡大地是沙門一隻眼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuefeng's recorded saying: the whole earth is a patch-robed monk's one eye.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大小雲門只具一隻眼。何故？只管瞻前，不管照後。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later appraisal says Yunmen has only one eye and gives its stated reason: he looks ahead but not behind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 刢利漢這裏著得一隻眼，便見七縱八橫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Instruction: an acute person who places one eye here sees seven ways vertically and eight horizontally.

Occurrences.Kwic: 拄杖子未免為諸人別開一隻眼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The teacher says his staff cannot avoid opening another eye for the assembly.

AlternateTargets: greatly awakened upon hearing the words
Senses.Explanation: A narrative formula: “at the words” or “under the words” (言下) plus “greatly awakened” (大悟). It occurs 542 times in 160 allowlisted texts and marks the reported moment immediately following a spoken exchange. The words vary from case to case. Daoxin is reported greatly awakened after Sengcan asks, “Who binds you?” and then, “Why seek release?”; Damei Fachang after Mazu says, “Mind itself is buddha” (即心是佛); Wuxie Lingmo after Shitou says, “From birth to death it is only this; why turn your head and move your brain?” (從生至死祇是者個，回頭轉腦作麼); Yanyang after Zhaozhou says, “If you cannot put it down, carry it away” (放不下，擔取去); and Huanglong Huinan after Ciming asks, “Do you take that as scolding?” (你作罵會那). What follows the formula also varies: the records may mention a bow, a verse, a reply, breaking a staff, residence with a teacher, or later teaching activity. The formula reports the event and its position after speech; it does not itself explain what was awakened to.
Senses.Note: Related narrative formulas show the same productive construction: “awakened at the words” (言下契悟), 41 hits in 28 texts; “suddenly awakened at the words” (言下頓悟), 65 in 40; “at the words, suddenly greatly awakened” (言下豁然大悟), 10 in 9; “thoroughly penetrated at the words” (言下大徹), 34 in 31; and “had an insight at the words” (言下有省), 215 in 89. These are related formulas, not alternate spellings of the four-character headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：誰縛汝？云：無人縛。師云：何更求解脫乎？信於言下大悟，服勤九載。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Sengcan section names the novice Daoxin as the person reported greatly awakened after this exchange.

Occurrences.Kwic: 明州大梅法常禪師襄陽鄭氏，予問馬大師：如何是佛？馬大師云：即心是佛。師於言下大悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Damei Fachang biography identifies Damei as the person reported greatly awakened after Mazu’s reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 頭曰：從生至死祇是者個，回頭轉腦作麼？洩言下大悟，乃抝折拄杖而棲止焉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Wuxie Lingmo case identifies Shitou as speaker and Wuxie as the person reported greatly awakened.

Occurrences.Kwic: 州曰：放不下，擔取去。陽於言下大悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing Yanyang case identifies Zhaozhou as speaker and Yanyang as the person reported awakened; Yanyang has no exact roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 山曰。龍袖拂開全體現。曰師意如何。山曰。象王行處絕狐踪。師於言下大悟拜起而曰。萬古碧潭空界月。再三撈摝始應知。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Shoushan Xingnian lineage section records Shoushan’s two replies, the disciple’s awakening, bow, and verse; the disciple’s roster identity is not safely supplied by the nearby lineage head.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：罵豈慈悲法施耶？明曰：你作罵會那？師於言下大悟，作頌曰：傑出叢林是趙州，老婆勘破沒來由。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Huanglong Huinan biography identifies Ciming as speaker and Huanglong as the person reported greatly awakened.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, before words or ahead of speech. The term occurs 338 times in 155 allowlisted texts. Its most visible Chan deployment is the paired formula 'discern before the words' and 'accord after the phrase.' Multiple records immediately refuse both positions: discerning before the words fails one's whole life, while according after the phrase departs from the body of the Way; Yuanwu similarly quotes discernment before words as still confined by a shell. The corpus also uses the phrase nominally for 'the matter before the words' and in a preface says the mind seal may be discerned before words. These are grammatical forms of the same temporal-relational phrase. They show a stock Chan axis for examining an answer's relation to spoken words, not a named realm or separate object.
Senses.Note: One relational sense. Nominal 'the matter before words,' adverbial 'discern before words,' and contrast with 'after the phrase' do not denote different things. The entry reports the corpus's paired verdicts without deciding what lies before speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 言前薦得，孤負平生。句後投機，全乖道體。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat statement gives the recurring before-words/after-phrase pair and rejects both.

Occurrences.Kwic: 言前薦得辜負平生句後投機殊乖道體離此二途請師方便師竪拂
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An older collected record preserves the pair in a public request and the master's raising of the whisk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 設使言前薦得。猶是滯殼迷封。縱饒句下精通。未免觸塗狂見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu quotes discernment before words and says it remains confined by a shell.

Occurrences.Kwic: 風穴下來言前事，舉似師，師云：維那！著什麼來由勸者漢？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp narrative uses the nominal expression 'the matter before the words.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 直指性宗，單傳心印，可得於眉睫，可薦於言前，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp-record preface says the mind seal may be discerned before words.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the road of language is cut off
AlternateTargets: the course of words is severed
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "the road" or "course" (道) of "language and words" (言語) is "cut off" (斷): "the road of language is cut off," attested 171 times in 71 allowlisted texts. It is most often paired with "the place of mental activity is extinguished" (心行處滅, 128 occurrences); the unpunctuated full pair occurs 12 times and the punctuated pair 17 times. The Trust in Mind verse places it in "trust in mind is not two; not two is trust in mind; the road of language is cut off; it is not past, future, or present" (信心不二，不二信心，言語道斷，非去來今). A lamp record gives an explicit correction: closing the eyes and seeing nothing in the dark is not what is called "the road of language is cut off" (不是閉目藏睛、暗覩無所見喚作言語道斷). A later address first quotes "it cannot be known by wisdom and cannot be recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished," then answers, "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and mental activity is not extinguished" (亦可以智知，亦可以識識，言語道斷，心行不滅). Hongzhi asks directly, "just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then?" (言語道斷心行處滅，又作麼生). The entry reports the fixed phrase, its paired formula, its correction, and its counter-formulation without turning silence or shut eyes into its definition.
Senses.Note: Dahui quotes a correspondent who says that looking at a saying leaves "the road of language cut off and the place of mental activity extinguished, with no words to say and no principle to advance" (看此話，直得言語道斷心行處滅，無言可說，無理可伸); the following context is Dahui's reply to that report, so the quoted claim is not assigned to him. The exact collocation "close the eyes and hide the pupils" (閉目藏睛) occurs 29 times, but the lamp record explicitly rejects it as the definition here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不可以智知，不可以識識，言語道斷，心行處滅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal address in Continued Essential Sayings of Ancient Worthies quotes: "it cannot be known by wisdom and cannot be recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished."

Occurrences.Kwic: 亦可以智知，亦可以識識，言語道斷，心行不滅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same address immediately supplies its counter-formulation: "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off and mental activity is not extinguished."

Occurrences.Kwic: 祇如言語道斷心行處滅。又作麼生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Hongzhi Zhengjue's record: "just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then?"

Occurrences.Kwic: 看此話。直得言語道斷心行處滅。無言可說。無理可伸。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's record quotes a correspondent: "looking at this saying, directly the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity extinguished; there are no words to say and no principle to advance." MasterName is null because these are the correspondent's words, not Dahui's.

Occurrences.Kwic: 信心不二。不二信心。言語道斷。非去來今。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Compendium of Five Lamps quotes the Trust in Mind verse in Sengcan's section: "trust in mind is not two; not two is trust in mind; the road of language is cut off; it is not past, future, or present." This is quoted verse, so MasterName is null.
